title: Ladder Networks
description: Reduce ladders from the far end, then walk the loaded dividers back to the output.

study.title: Anatomy of a ladder
study.body: A ladder alternates **series** resistors along the top rail with **shunt** resistors (rungs) to the bottom rail. To find $R_{in}$, start at the end **farthest** from the source: add series, combine with the rung in parallel, and repeat toward the source.

study.title: Walking back to the output
study.body: Once $R_{in}$ gives you the first node voltage, every section is a voltage divider between its series resistor and **everything to the right of it** (already reduced). Multiply the divider ratios section by section to reach $v_{out}$.

study.title: Shortcut: the unit-output trick
study.body: Circuits made of resistors and sources are linear: doubling the source doubles every voltage and current. So assume $v_{out}$ = 1 V, work **backward** to the source with Ohm's law and KCL, and find the source voltage this needs. Then scale every result by the real $V_s$ divided by that value.

study.title: Common mistakes
study.body:
- Multiplying 'unloaded' divider ratios: each divider is loaded by the rest of the ladder, so use $R_{right}$, not the single rung.
- Treating the last series resistor as carrying current when the output is open: with nothing connected, the last series resistor and the last rung carry the **same** current.
- Starting the reduction at the source end instead of the far end.

steps.prompt: Two-rung ladder; all values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the input resistance seen by the source.
ask.explanation: From the far end: $R_3+R_4$ = {{R3+R4|Ω}}, parallel with $R_2$: {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}, plus $R_1$: $R_{in}$ = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the node voltage $v_1$.
ask.explanation: $R_{right} = R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)$ = {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}. Divider: $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_{right}}{R_1+R_{right}}$ = **{{v_v_1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the output voltage $v_{out}$.
ask.explanation: First $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)}{R_1+R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)}$ = {{v_v_1|V}}. Then $v_{out} = v_1\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$ = **{{v_v_out|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current in the first rung, $R_2$.

steps.explanation: That would be true only if all four resistors were in series. $R_2$ is a rung that takes current away, so first find $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)}{R_1 + R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)}$ and then $v_{out} = v_1\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$.

steps.prompt: A current source drives a two-rung ladder.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage across the current source.
ask.explanation: The source sees $R_1\parallel(R_2+R_3)$ = {{R1|Ω}} ∥ {{R2+R3|Ω}} = {{par(R1,R2+R3)|Ω}}, so $V = I_sR$ = **{{V_Is|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the output voltage $v_{out}$.
ask.explanation: The current divider sends $I_s\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2+R_3}$ = {{abs(I_R3)|A}} through $R_2$ and $R_3$, so $v_{out} = I\,R_3$ = **{{v_v_out|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current in the rung $R_1$.

steps.prompt: Where do you start when reducing a ladder to its input resistance?
options: At the end farthest from the source
steps.explanation: Only at the far end do you know what each resistor is connected to: the last series resistor and the last rung are simply in series. Combine, put the result in parallel with the next rung, add the next series resistor, and so on toward the source.

steps.prompt: You reduce this ladder to find $R_{eq}$ seen by the source. Tap the **two** resistors you combine first.
steps.explanation:
Start at the end **farthest from the source**. $R_5$ and $R_6$ carry the same current (nothing else is connected at their joint), so they are in series: $R_5 + R_6$. Then work back towards the source:
$$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 \parallel \big(R_3 + R_4 \parallel (R_5 + R_6)\big)$$
$R_1$ is in series with the source, but you can only add it at the very end, once everything behind it is one resistor.

steps.prompt: The ladder's source voltage $V_s$ is unknown.

ask.prompt: What source voltage $V_s$ gives $v_{out}$ = {{Vt|V}}?
ask.explanation: Work backward from the output: $I_4 = v_{out}/R_4$, $v_1 = v_{out} + I_4R_3$ = {{Vt*(R3+R4)/R4|V}}, $I_1 = I_4 + v_1/R_2$ = {{Vt/R4 + Vt*(R3+R4)/R4/R2|A}}, and $V_s = v_1 + I_1R_1$ = **{{Vt/v_v_out|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the ratio $v_{out}/V_s$.
ask.explanation: $\frac{v_{out}}{V_s} = \frac{R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)}{R_1+R_2\parallel(R_3+R_4)}\cdot\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$ = {{par(R2,R3+R4)/(R1+par(R2,R3+R4))||3}} · {{R4/(R3+R4)||3}} = **{{v_v_out||3}}**. It does not depend on $V_s$.

steps.hint: Linearity: the ratio $v_{out}/V_s$ is fixed by the resistors.

steps.prompt: With nothing connected to the output, $R_3$ and $R_4$ carry the same current.
steps.explanation: The output terminal is open, so the node between $R_3$ and $R_4$ has only those two elements: KCL says they carry the same current, and $R_3$, $R_4$ are in series.

steps.prompt: Three-rung ladder; all values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: Find the input resistance seen by the source.
Find the middle node voltage $v_2$.
Find the output voltage $v_{out}$.
ask.explanation: $v_1$ = {{v_v_1|V}} and $v_2$ = {{v_v_2|V}} (dividers with the loaded sections). Last section: $v_{out} = v_2\frac{R_6}{R_5+R_6}$ = **{{v_v_out|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current in the rung $R_4$.

steps.prompt: An R–2R ladder: series resistors $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, rungs and termination $2R$.

ask.prompt: Find $v_3$.
ask.explanation: Looking right from $v_3$: $2R\parallel2R = R$. So from $v_2$ the series $R$ sees $R$: $v_3 = v_2/2$, and the same happens one section earlier: $v_2 = V_s/2$. Hence $v_3 = V_s/4$ = **{{v_v_3|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current supplied by the source.
ask.explanation: Every 'look to the right' gives $2R\parallel 2R = R$, so the source sees $R_{in} = R$ = {{R|Ω}}: $I = V_s/R$ = **{{I_Vs|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current through the termination resistor $R_6$.

steps.prompt: In a correctly terminated R–2R ladder, each node voltage compared with the node before it is…
steps.explanation: The resistance looking right from every node is $2R\parallel2R = R$, so each series $R$ forms a 1:1 divider with that $R$: every step halves the voltage. This is how R–2R digital-to-analog converters produce binary weights.

steps.prompt: A current source drives a three-rung ladder.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage across the current source.
Find $v_2$.
ask.explanation: $V$ = {{V_Is|V}} across the source. Divider into the next section: $v_2 = V\frac{R_3\parallel(R_4+R_5)}{R_2+R_3\parallel(R_4+R_5)}$ = **{{v_v_2|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the output voltage $v_{out}$.
ask.explanation: $v_2$ = {{v_v_2|V}} (see the divider from the source node). Then $v_{out} = v_2\frac{R_5}{R_4+R_5}$ = **{{v_v_out|V}}**.

steps.prompt: If $V_s$ is doubled, every current in a resistor ladder doubles.
steps.explanation: A network of resistors and one independent source is linear: all voltages and currents are proportional to the source. That is exactly why the unit-output trick works.

steps.prompt: The switch S is closed and shorts the output of the ladder.

ask.prompt: Find the input resistance seen by the source.
ask.explanation: The closed switch shorts $R_4$, so the far end is just $R_3$: $R_{in} = R_1 + R_2\parallel R_3$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}} = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current through the switch.
ask.explanation: $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_2\parallel R_3}{R_1+R_2\parallel R_3}$ = {{v_v_1|V}}. All of the current in $R_3$ goes through the switch (none through the shorted $R_4$): $I = v_1/R_3$ = **{{abs(I_S1)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: The source voltage of this three-rung ladder is unknown.

ask.prompt: What source voltage $V_s$ gives $v_{out}$ = {{Vt|V}}?
Find the voltage ratio $v_{out}/V_s$.

steps.prompt: The ladder's output is brought out to terminals a and b.

ask.prompt: Find the input resistance seen by the source (a–b open).
With $V_s$ replaced by a short circuit, find the resistance looking into terminals a–b.
ask.explanation: Now reduce from the source end: $R_1\parallel R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}; + $R_3$: {{R3+par(R1,R2)|Ω}}; ∥ $R_4$: {{par(R4,R3+par(R1,R2))|Ω}}; + $R_5$: {{R5+par(R4,R3+par(R1,R2))|Ω}}; ∥ $R_6$: **{{Req|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the open-circuit voltage $v_{ab}$.
ask.explanation: Open output: the loaded dividers give $v_1$ = {{v_v_1|V}}, $v_2$ = {{v_v_2|V}}, and $v_{ab} = v_2\frac{R_6}{R_5+R_6}$ = **{{Voc|V}}**.

steps.hint: The resistance seen depends on which end you look into.

steps.prompt: Order the steps of the unit-output (backward) method for a ladder.
items: Find the last rung's current and the next node voltage back
Repeat KCL and Ohm's law section by section to the source
Scale all results by $V_s$ divided by the source voltage you found
steps.explanation: Working backward avoids nested parallel combinations: each step uses only Ohm's law and KCL. Because the circuit is linear, scaling the assumed solution by the ratio of the real to the 'needed' source voltage gives the true values.

steps.prompt: Three-rung ladder; all values are shown in the schematic.

ask.prompt: What percentage of the source power reaches the last rung $R_6$?
ask.explanation: $v_{out}$ = {{v_v_out|V}}, so $P_{R_6} = v_{out}^2/R_6$ = {{P_R6|W}}. The source delivers $V_sI$ = {{P_Vs|W}} ($R_{in}$ = {{(R1+par(R2,(R3+par(R4,(R5+R6)))))|Ω}}). Ratio: **{{100*P_R6/P_Vs|%}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the power absorbed by $R_1$.
ask.explanation: $R_1$ carries the full input current $V_s/R_{in}$ = {{Vs|V}} / {{(R1+par(R2,(R3+par(R4,(R5+R6)))))|Ω}} = {{I_Vs|A}}, so $P = I^2R_1$ = **{{P_R1|W}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current through $R_3$.
ask.explanation: $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_{right,1}}{R_1+R_{right,1}}$ = {{v_v_1|V}} with $R_{right,1}$ = {{par(R2,(R3+par(R4,(R5+R6))))|Ω}}. $R_3$ feeds everything to its right ({{(R3+par(R4,(R5+R6)))|Ω}} including itself): $I = v_1/(R_3 + R_4\parallel(R_5+R_6))$ = **{{abs(I_R3)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: A fourth rung (series resistor + shunt resistor) is added at the output end of a ladder. The input resistance seen by the source…
steps.explanation: The new section is connected in parallel with the old last rung, which lowers that rung's effective resistance. That lower value propagates through every series/parallel step toward the source, so $R_{in}$ decreases (usually only slightly).

steps.prompt: The closed switch S connects the middle node $v_2$ to the bottom rail.

ask.prompt: Find the current through the switch.
ask.explanation: The switch holds $v_2$ = 0, so $R_4$, $R_5$, $R_6$ carry nothing. $R_{in} = R_1 + R_2\parallel R_3$ = {{R1+par(R2,R3)|Ω}}, $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_2\parallel R_3}{R_{in}}$ = {{v_v_1|V}}, and the switch carries $v_1/R_3$ = **{{abs(I_S1)|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the node voltage $v_1$.
ask.explanation: With $v_2$ shorted to the rail, $R_3$ goes straight to ground and the rest of the ladder is dead. $v_1 = V_s\frac{R_2\parallel R_3}{R_1+R_2\parallel R_3}$ = **{{v_v_1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the power delivered by the source.
ask.explanation: $R_{in} = R_1 + R_2\parallel R_3$ = {{R1+par(R2,R3)|Ω}} (everything beyond the switch is shorted out), so $P = V_s^2/R_{in}$ = **{{P_Vs|W}}**.
